Sickness
sĭck´ness
n. (disease, ill health; rendering Hebrew choli, machalah, Greek astheneia, nosos)
From Anglo-Saxon seoc, ill. Scripture treats sickness as a real intruder from the fall, under God's hand, and never as a mere mechanism.

Biblical Definition

Sickness in Scripture is neither meaningless nor simply punitive. It stands under God's government: He promises to take sickness from the midst of an obedient Israel (Exo 23:25; Deu 7:15) and threatens it in the covenant curses (Deu 28:61). But the canon carefully forbids the flat inference that sickness proves personal sin. Elisha, the prophet of God, “was fallen sick of his sickness whereof he died” (2Ki 13:14) — a faithful man, a fatal illness, no rebuke attached. Asa's case supplies the actual warning, and it is not about medicine: “in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians” (2Ch 16:12). The fault was the order, not the doctors. The gospel then reveals where sickness is finally dealt with: “Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses” (Mat 8:17). And James gives the church its ordinary practice — call for the elders, and let them pray (Jas 5:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines sickness as disease, illness, or a morbid state of the body, and notes its figurative use for a disordered state of anything — the sickness of a nation or of the heart.

expand to see more

SICK´NESS, n. Disease; illness; the state of being diseased; the state of the body in which its functions are disturbed or deranged.

2. A particular disease; as a fatal sickness.

3. Nausea; a disposition to vomit.

4. A disordered state; as the sickness of the heart.

Key Scripture

Mat 8:17 — "That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses."

2Ch 16:12 — "And Asa in the thirty and ninth year of his reign was diseased in his feet, until his disease was exceeding great: yet in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians."

2Ki 13:14 — "Now Elisha was fallen sick of his sickness whereof he died. And Joash the king of Israel came down unto him, and wept over his face, and said, O my father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof."

Jas 5:14 — "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord:"

Modern Corruption

Two errors from one root — the faith-healing teaching that makes sickness a proof of unbelief, and the secular reading that empties it of any meaning at all.

expand to see more

The prosperity and faith-healing movements teach that healing is guaranteed in the atonement for this life, so that continuing sickness convicts the sufferer of insufficient faith. It is a cruel doctrine and the text refutes it: Elisha died of his sickness; Paul left Trophimus at Miletum sick; Timothy was told to take a little wine for his often infirmities; and Paul's own thorn was not removed but answered with sufficient grace. Matthew 8:17 is true and its full harvest is eschatological — the tomb is empty and the graves are not yet.

The opposite error strips sickness of meaning entirely, leaving only biology and management. Scripture will not have that either. Asa is the case in point, and the point is frequently mistaken: he is not condemned for consulting physicians but for seeking them and not the LORD. Means are legitimate; means without prayer are Asa's error. James 5:14 shows the ordinary Christian practice that holds both together — the elders, prayer, and oil, in the name of the Lord.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew choli (H2483), sickness, from chalah, to be weak — the word of Isaiah 53's Man of sorrows; Greek astheneia (G769), want of strength; nosos (G3554), disease.

expand to see more

Hebrew choli (H2483) — sickness, grief; in Isa 53:3 the Servant is acquainted with grief, literally with sickness.

Hebrew machalah (H4245) — disease, infirmity; the sickness the LORD promises to take from Israel's midst (Exo 23:25).

Greek astheneia (G769) — weakness, infirmity, sickness; Matthew applies it to Christ bearing our infirmities (Mat 8:17).

Usage

"“Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses” — true, and its full harvest is not yet."

"“In his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians” — the fault was the order."

"“Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders” — the church's ordinary practice."
